Chapter 5 · History · India and the Contemporary World II

Print Culture and the Modern World

Print did not just spread ideas; it created a new kind of reader. This chapter follows printing from woodblocks in China through Gutenberg, the Reformation, the reading mania and the nineteenth-century press in India, where print became a weapon of reform and of nationalism.

Chapter Overview

What this chapter is about, at a glance

Print began in China, where hand printing from woodblocks was known from about AD 594. Buddhist missionaries carried it to Japan, and the earliest printed book, the Diamond Sutra of 868, was produced there. In China and Japan, print was used for examination texts, religious images and illustrated books, and in Japan a lively urban culture produced the ukiyo prints of artists such as Kitagawa Utamaro and Hokusai.

Marco Polo brought knowledge of woodblock printing back to Italy in 1295, and by the fifteenth century woodblock printing had reached Europe. Then Johannes Gutenberg developed the printing press in the 1430s, using metal movable type and an oil-based ink, and produced his famous Bible — about 180 copies in three years. Print made books cheap and abundant, created a new reading public, and shook the authority of the Church: Martin Luther’s Ninety Five Theses (1517) were printed and circulated widely, and the Catholic Church responded with the Index of Prohibited Books (1558).

The seventeenth and eighteenth centuries saw a “reading mania” — almanacs, ballads, chapbooks, newspapers, journals and, from 1751, Diderot’s Encyclopaedia. In the nineteenth century print reached children, women and workers through fairy tales, novels, penny magazines and lending libraries, and technical innovations — the power-driven press, offset printing, the linotype and colour printing — made printed matter ever cheaper.

In India, print arrived with the British: James Augustus Hickey’s Bengal Gazette (1780) was the first newspaper, and a vigorous vernacular press followed — Ram Mohan Roy’s Sambad Kaumudi (1821), Mirat-ul-Akhbar (1822), Tilak’s Kesari and Amrita Bazar Patrika. Print carried religious and social reform, gave women and lower castes a voice, and became a weapon of nationalism — which is why the colonial government passed the Vernacular Press Act of 1878.

Woodblock printing

A method of printing in which a full page is carved on a block of wood, inked and pressed on paper — used in China from about AD 594.

Movable type

Individual letters cast in metal, which could be rearranged to set any text — the basis of Gutenberg’s method.

Printing press

Gutenberg’s press of the 1430s, which pressed inked type on to paper and made books cheap and abundant.

Vellum

A parchment made from the skin of animals, used for manuscripts before paper became common.

Chapbook

A small, cheap booklet sold by pedlars, containing ballads, folk tales and popular stories.

Bibliothèque Bleue

A series of cheap, small books in France, sold by pedlars and read widely by ordinary people.

Index of Prohibited Books

A list of books banned by the Catholic Church, first issued in 1558, to control what people read.

Ukiyo

Japanese woodblock prints of the “floating world” — urban life, theatre and pleasure districts.

Vernacular Press Act 1878

The Act that allowed the government to censor and control newspapers printed in Indian languages.

Manuscript

A hand-written document, produced before the age of print, often on palm leaf or handmade paper.

The First Printed Books — China and Japan

The earliest kind of print technology was developed in China, Japan and Korea. From AD 594 onwards, books in China were printed by rubbing paper against the inked surface of woodblocks. As both sides of the thin, porous sheet could not be printed, the traditional Chinese “accordion book” was folded and stitched at the side. Superbly skilled craftsmen could duplicate, with remarkable accuracy, the beauty of calligraphy.

The imperial state in China was, for a very long time, the major producer of printed material. China possessed a huge bureaucratic system which recruited its personnel through civil service examinations, and textbooks for this examination were printed in vast numbers under the sponsorship of the imperial state. From the sixteenth century, the number of examination candidates went up and that increased the volume of print.

By the seventeenth century, as urban culture bloomed in China, the uses of print diversified. Print was no longer used just by scholar-officials; merchants used print in their everyday life, to collect trade information. Reading became a leisure activity, and new forms of literature — fiction, poetry, autobiographies, romantic plays — became popular. Wives of scholar-officials published their works and courtesans wrote about their lives.

Japan

Buddhist missionaries from China introduced hand-printing technology into Japan around AD 768–770, to print Buddhist scriptures for the monastery. The oldest printed book in Japan is the Diamond Sutra, dated AD 868. It contains woodcut illustrations and text, and was printed for free distribution.

The Japanese were the first to use movable type, in the late sixteenth century, but it was not widely used because their language had many characters. Woodblock printing remained common, and by the mid-eighteenth century a lively urban culture developed around it. Printers produced ukiyo (“pictures of the floating world”) prints — images of urban life, theatre, teahouses and pleasure quarters — and artists such as Kitagawa Utamaro (c. 1753–1806) and Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1849) became famous. Hokusai’s “Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji” included the celebrated “The Great Wave”.

Print Comes to Europe

For centuries, silk and spices from China flowed into Europe through the silk route, and with them came woodblock printing. It was Marco Polo, a great explorer, who returned to Italy in 1295 after years of exploration in China, and brought back with him the knowledge of woodblock printing. Soon, Italian began producing books with woodblocks, and the technology spread to other parts of Europe.

Luxury editions were still handwritten on very expensive vellum, bound beautifully and meant for the rich and the aristocracy. As the demand for books increased, booksellers all over Europe began exporting books to many different countries. Book fairs were held at different places, and production of handwritten manuscripts was organised in new workshops or factories to meet the demand.

But handwritten manuscripts could not satisfy the ever-increasing demand for books: they were expensive, fragile and slow to produce, and copying was a laborious process. So the need for a cheaper and faster method of reproduction was felt, and this led to the invention of the printing press.

Gutenberg and the printing press

Gutenberg

Johannes Gutenberg grew up in a large agricultural estate and learnt the art of polishing stones, became a master goldsmith and acquired expertise in creating lead moulds. By 1448 he had perfected his system: he used his knowledge to design movable type — individual letters cast in metal — and adapted the existing technology of the olive press to make a printing press. He used an oil-based ink and a metal mould to cast type. His first printed book was the Bible: about 180 copies in three years, compared with the years a single handwritten copy would take.

The new technology did not entirely displace the existing art of producing books by hand. In fact, printed books at first closely resembled the written manuscripts in appearance and layout: the metal letters imitated the ornamental handwritten styles, borders were illuminated by hand and illustrations painted. In the books printed for the rich, space for decoration was kept blank on the printed page for the buyer to choose the design and the painting.

Between 1450 and 1550, printing presses were set up in most countries of Europe. Printers from Germany travelled to other countries seeking work and helping start new presses. As the number of printing presses grew, book production boomed: the second half of the fifteenth century saw 20 million copies of printed books flooding the markets in Europe, and the number went up to about 200 million copies in the sixteenth century.

The Print Revolution and Its Impact

The shift from hand printing to mechanical printing is called the print revolution. It changed the relationship of people to information and knowledge, and it changed the relationship of readers to authors and authorities.

A new reading public

Print created a new reading public. Before print, reading was confined to the elite — the Church, the aristocracy and the scholars — and books were expensive. Print made books cheap, so a new reading public emerged that was far larger and more varied. But this did not happen all at once: in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the reading public was still small, and literacy was limited. Between the literate and the illiterate there grew an intermediate world of oral culture — ballads, folk tales and songs were printed and read aloud, so that even the illiterate could participate.

Printers began to publish cheap small books — chapbooks and the French Bibliothèque Bleue — which were sold by pedlars and read widely. Ballads and folk tales were printed and sold, and the oral and the printed cultures fed on each other.

Religious debates and the Reformation

Print did not only stimulate the publication of conflicting opinions; it also permitted the wider circulation of ideas, and so it shaped the Reformation. Martin Luther, a German monk, was outraged by the practices of the Catholic Church — particularly the sale of indulgences — and in 1517 he wrote his Ninety Five Theses, criticising the Church. Printed copies of the Theses spread rapidly across Europe, and Luther’s translation of the Bible into German made the scriptures available to ordinary people. Luther said, “Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one.”

The Church did not accept this quietly. It began to maintain an Index of Prohibited Books from 1558, and it tried to control what was printed and read. Erasmus, the humanist scholar, feared that the printed book would produce “a world of books” in which the bad would drive out the good, and he doubted whether print would make people wiser. He was not alone in his anxiety: many feared that print would spread sedition, irreligion and rebellion.

Print also created new forms of reading and new readers. The Italian miller Menocchio, a sixteenth-century reader, read printed books and formed his own ideas about the universe, which brought him before the Inquisition. His case shows that print allowed ordinary people to read, interpret and question in ways that had not been possible when books were rare.

The Reading Mania

The seventeenth and eighteenth centuries saw a “reading mania” in Europe. Churches of different denominations set up schools in villages, so that by the mid-eighteenth century literacy rates in many parts of Europe were as high as 60 to 80 per cent. New forms of popular literature appeared, targeted at new readers, who could be found among traders and shopkeepers as well as among the poorer sections of society.

  • Almanacs, calendars and journals were printed and sold widely; almanacs combined information about the seasons, the stars and the weather with entertainment.
  • Ballads, folk tales and chapbooks were sold by pedlars, who carried them from village to village.
  • Newspapers and periodicals appeared, first weekly and then daily, and were read in coffee houses and read aloud to the illiterate.
  • The Bibliothèque Bleue in France and similar series elsewhere made cheap books available to ordinary readers.
  • Scientific and scholarly works were printed — Isaac Newton’s work, and from 1751 Denis Diderot’s Encyclopaedia, a massive project that ran to 28 volumes and spread the ideas of the Enlightenment.

The reading mania had political consequences. Print made possible the rapid circulation of criticism of the monarchy and the Church, and it created a public sphere in which ideas of liberty, reason and equality could be debated. Historians have argued that print helped prepare the ground for the French Revolution of 1789, as pamphlets, newspapers and books spread the ideas of the Enlightenment to a wide audience.

The Nineteenth Century — Children, Women and Workers

In the nineteenth century, print reached new groups of readers. Children’s literature grew: the Grimm brothers collected and published folk tales, and books were written especially for children. Women became both readers and writers — Jane Austen, the Brontë sisters, George Eliot and many others wrote novels that were read widely, and women also wrote for magazines and journals.

Workers gained access to print through cheap books, penny magazines, serialised novels and lending libraries. In Britain, the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge and similar bodies published cheap educational literature; workers’ libraries and reading rooms were set up; and the serialised novel made fiction affordable, since a story could be bought in weekly parts.

This was also the age of reform: print carried the arguments of the anti-slavery movement, the campaign for factory legislation, the demand for the vote and the temperance movement. Print made possible the great public campaigns of the nineteenth century, with pamphlets, posters and newspapers reaching a mass audience.

Further Innovations

Print technology was improved through the nineteenth century, and each improvement made printed matter cheaper and more abundant:

Innovations in printing
InnovationWhenEffect
Power-driven printing press (Richard Hoe)1840sMuch faster printing of large editions
Offset pressLate nineteenth centuryAllowed printing on a cylindrical surface and finer reproduction
Linotype machine1880sSet type mechanically instead of by hand
Photo-electric control and colour printing1920sFaster, cheaper and coloured printing
Cheap paperback1930sBooks affordable for a mass readership

These innovations, together with cheaper paper and faster transport, made the mass circulation of newspapers and books possible — and made print the dominant medium of the modern world.

India and the World of Print

Before print, India had a rich manuscript culture. Manuscripts were written by hand on palm leaves and on handmade paper, in Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic and the regional languages. They were expensive and fragile, and they had to be handled carefully; they could not be read easily, since the script was written in different styles. Manuscripts were copied by scribes, and their production was slow.

Print came to India with the Europeans. The Portuguese missionaries brought the printing press to Goa in the mid-sixteenth century, and the first book printed in India was in Portuguese. But the real growth of the Indian press came with the British in the late eighteenth century.

The first newspapers

James Augustus Hickey began publishing the Bengal Gazette in 1780 — the first newspaper in India — and it was followed by other papers. These early papers were published by Europeans and were read mainly by Europeans, but they established the idea of a regular printed news publication.

The vernacular press

The growth of the vernacular press was the decisive development. Raja Ram Mohan Roy started Sambad Kaumudi in 1821, and the first issue of Mirat-ul-Akhbar, a Persian newspaper, appeared in 1822. Other papers followed in Bengali, Hindi, Marathi, Tamil, Telugu and other languages, and by the second half of the nineteenth century the vernacular press had become a powerful force.

The vernacular press did three things: it carried news and information to readers who did not know English; it created a public sphere in which political and social questions could be debated; and it gave voice to Indian opinion against colonial rule. Papers such as Kesari (edited by Bal Gangadhar Tilak), Amrita Bazar Patrika, The Hindu and The Tribune became vehicles of nationalism.

Religious Reform and Public Debates

Print was central to the religious reform movements of the nineteenth century. Reformers used newspapers, pamphlets and books to argue for change and to reach a wide audience, and their opponents used the same means to reply.

Raja Ram Mohan Roy used print to campaign against sati and for the reform of Hinduism, and his Sambad Kaumudi carried these arguments. Dayanand Saraswati, founder of the Arya Samaj, published his views and attracted followers; Swami Vivekananda’s lectures and writings were printed and circulated widely, and his works reached readers across India and abroad.

Among Muslims, the ulama used print to spread their teachings: the Deoband seminary, founded in 1867, published fatwas — legal opinions — which were printed and distributed to guide Muslims on religious matters. Sir Syed Ahmed Khan founded the Aligarh movement and published Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq (“The Mohammedan Social Reformer”) to promote modern education and reform.

Print thus made religious debate public. Arguments that had been conducted among scholars were now carried on in newspapers and pamphlets, in front of a reading public, and this widened both the audience and the intensity of the debates.

Print and the Poor, and Women’s Voices

Print also gave a voice to those who had been excluded from public life. Jyotiba Phule, the Maratha pioneer of “low caste” protest movements, wrote about the injustice of the caste system in his book Gulamgiri, published in 1871, and he dedicated it to the American slaves who had been freed. Dr B.R. Ambedkar wrote extensively against caste and for the rights of the Depressed Classes, and his writings were printed and circulated widely. In Madras, E.V. Ramaswamy Periyar published Kudi Arasu to attack caste and Brahminical dominance.

Women’s writing was one of the most remarkable products of print culture. Rashsundari Debi, a woman from a conservative family in Bengal, learnt to read in secret and wrote her autobiography Amar Jiban (“My Life”), published in 1876 — the first full-length autobiography published in the Bengali language. Tarabai Shinde published Stripurushtulna (“A Comparison between Women and Men”) in 1882, attacking the social differences between men and women. Pandita Ramabai wrote about the miserable lives of upper-caste Hindu women and founded a widow’s home at Pune. Kailashbashini Debi wrote about the experiences of women — how women were imprisoned at home, kept in ignorance and forced to do hard domestic labour.

In Maharashtra, Ram Chaddha published Istri Dharm Vichar, a conduct book for women, and in Punjab, Bhai Vir Singh wrote and published works that shaped a new Punjabi literature. Print thus created a space in which women could describe their own lives — a space that had not existed before.

Print and Censorship

As print grew, so did the colonial government’s anxiety about it. The vernacular press was critical of British rule, and the government responded with control.

The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 allowed the government to censor reports and editorials in the vernacular press. If a vernacular newspaper published anything that was considered “seditious”, the government could warn the editor, seize the press and machinery, and confiscate the property. The Act was aimed at papers printed in Indian languages, while English-language papers were left comparatively free — a discrimination that Indian nationalists bitterly criticised.

Despite the Act, nationalist newspapers continued to publish, and print became more, not less, central to the national movement. Gandhiji linked the freedom of the press to political freedom: he said that “the fight for Swaraj is a fight for liberty of speech, liberty of the press, and freedom of association” — the freedom to criticise, to argue and to organise could not be separated from the freedom of the nation.

Print thus did two things at once in India: it created a national public — readers who, in different languages and different provinces, followed the same debates — and it gave them the means to organise. That is why the chapter ends with the press, and why censorship is the test of a free society.

NCERT In-text Questions and Answers

The questions printed inside the chapter

These are the “Can you…” and activity questions that appear inside the chapter text. Model answers are based on the chapter itself.

1.

Give reasons for the following: (a) Woodblock print only came to Europe after 1295 (b) Martin Luther was in favour of print and spoke out in praise of it (c) The Roman Catholic Church began keeping an Index of Prohibited Books from the mid-sixteenth century (d) Gandhi said the fight for Swaraj is a fight for liberty of speech, liberty of the press and freedom of association.

Model answer

(a) Because it was Marco Polo who returned to Italy in 1295 after years in China and brought back knowledge of woodblock printing; before that, Europe relied on handwritten manuscripts on vellum. (b) Because print allowed his Ninety Five Theses and his German translation of the Bible to circulate widely and cheaply, so his criticism of the Church could reach ordinary people — he called printing “the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one”. (c) Because print made it possible for criticism of the Church to spread rapidly; the Index was an attempt to control what people read and to suppress writings the Church considered heretical. (d) Because freedom of speech, press and association are the substance of political freedom: without the freedom to criticise, argue and organise, a nation cannot demand or sustain self-rule. The press was the instrument through which Indians debated and organised, which is why the colonial state tried to control it.

2.

Write short notes on: (a) The Gutenberg Press (b) Erasmus’s idea of the printed book (c) The Vernacular Press Act.

Model answer

(a) Gutenberg Press: developed in the 1430s by Johannes Gutenberg, a German goldsmith; it used metal movable type, an oil-based ink and the mechanism of the olive press. His first book was the Bible — about 180 copies in three years. Printed books at first imitated manuscripts in appearance, with hand-painted initials and borders. (b) Erasmus: the humanist scholar welcomed print but feared its effects — he worried that the printed book would produce “a world of books” in which the bad would drive out the good, and he doubted that print alone would make people wiser. (c) Vernacular Press Act: passed in 1878, it allowed the government to censor reports and editorials in Indian-language newspapers; a “seditious” publication could be warned, its press and machinery seized and its property confiscated. English-language papers were left comparatively free, which nationalists criticised as discriminatory.

3.

Write about the ways in which the print culture assisted the growth of nationalism in India.

Model answer

Print created a national public: newspapers in Bengali, Hindi, Marathi, Tamil and other languages carried the same news and debates to readers across provinces, so that people who had never met began to follow the same questions. It spread the arguments of nationalism — Tilak’s Kesari, Amrita Bazar Patrika, The Hindu and The Tribune carried criticism of colonial policy and news of movements. It carried the message of social reform, which prepared a modern, self-critical public. It gave women, dalits and the poor a voice, widening the nation beyond the elite. And it made organisation possible: notices of meetings, reports of speeches, pamphlets and petitions could be circulated quickly. That is why the government feared the vernacular press and passed the Vernacular Press Act.

4.

How did print culture help in bringing about the Reformation in Europe?

Model answer

Print allowed criticism of the Church to circulate quickly and cheaply. Luther’s Ninety Five Theses (1517) were printed and spread across Europe within weeks; his German translation of the Bible put the scriptures in the hands of ordinary readers, who could now interpret them without the mediation of priests. Print also produced pamphlets and tracts in which reformers and their opponents argued in public, and it created a reading public that could judge the arguments for itself. The Church’s response — the Index of Prohibited Books (1558) — shows how serious the threat was.

5.

How did the printing press become a tool of social change in nineteenth-century India?

Model answer

It allowed reformers to argue publicly and repeatedly: Ram Mohan Roy’s campaign against sati, Dayanand Saraswati’s Arya Samaj, Vivekananda’s writings, Sir Syed Ahmed Khan’s Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq and the Deoband fatwas all depended on print. It gave the excluded a platform: Jyotiba Phule’s Gulamgiri (1871), Ambedkar’s writings, Periyar’s Kudi Arasu, and women’s writing such as Rashsundari Debi’s Amar Jiban (1876) and Tarabai Shinde’s Stripurushtulna (1882). And it made the reform arguments national, since a pamphlet written in one province could be read in another. Social change in the nineteenth century was, to a large extent, an argument conducted in print.

6.

Why did the reading public grow in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries?

Model answer

Because print made books and pamphlets cheap, and churches of different denominations set up village schools, so that by the mid-eighteenth century literacy in parts of Europe reached 60 to 80 per cent. New forms of popular literature — almanacs, ballads, chapbooks, newspapers and journals — were produced for these new readers, and coffee houses and reading aloud brought print even to the illiterate.

7.

What was the “reading mania”?

Model answer

The explosion of popular reading in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Europe, when cheap print — almanacs, calendars, ballads, chapbooks, newspapers and journals — reached traders, shopkeepers and poorer readers, and literacy rose sharply. It created a public sphere in which ideas of reason, liberty and equality circulated, and historians link it to the Enlightenment and to the French Revolution.

8.

How did print change the lives of women in India?

Model answer

It gave them a means to write and be read. Rashsundari Debi learnt to read in secret and published her autobiography Amar Jiban (1876), the first full-length autobiography in Bengali; Tarabai Shinde published Stripurushtulna (1882) comparing the condition of women and men; Pandita Ramabai wrote about the lives of upper-caste Hindu women and founded a widow’s home; Kailashbashini Debi wrote about women imprisoned at home and kept in ignorance. Print created a space in which women could describe their own lives — and in which other women could read about them.

9.

What was the role of print in the religious debates of nineteenth-century India?

Model answer

Print made religious debate public. Reformers — Ram Mohan Roy, Dayanand Saraswati, Vivekananda — used newspapers, pamphlets and books to argue for change; the ulama used print to spread their teachings, with the Deoband seminary (1867) printing fatwas for distribution; and Sir Syed Ahmed Khan used Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq to promote modern education and reform. Arguments once confined to scholars were now conducted before a reading public, which widened both the audience and the intensity of the debates.

10.

Why was the Vernacular Press Act passed, and what did it do?

Model answer

Because the vernacular press had become critical of British rule and had begun to shape Indian public opinion. The Act of 1878 allowed the government to censor reports and editorials in Indian-language newspapers; a “seditious” publication could be warned, its press and machinery seized and its property confiscated. English-language papers were left comparatively free, which nationalists saw as a discrimination against Indian opinion.

1.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Give reasons for the following: (a) Woodblock print only came to Europe after 1295 (b) Martin Luther was in favour of print and spoke out in praise of it (c) The Roman Catholic Church began keeping an Index of Prohibited Books from the mid-sixteenth century (d) Gandhi said the fight for Swaraj is a fight for liberty of speech, liberty of the press and freedom of association.

Model answer

(a) Because Marco Polo brought knowledge of woodblock printing to Italy in 1295 after his travels in China. (b) Because print let his Theses and his German Bible reach ordinary readers cheaply — he called printing the ultimate gift of God. (c) Because print allowed criticism of the Church to circulate rapidly, and the Index was an attempt to control what people read. (d) Because freedom of speech, press and association are the substance of political freedom — without them a nation cannot criticise, debate or organise, and so cannot win or keep self-rule.

2.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Write short notes on: (a) The Gutenberg Press (b) Erasmus’s idea of the printed book (c) The Vernacular Press Act.

Model answer

(a) Gutenberg’s press of the 1430s used metal movable type, oil-based ink and the mechanism of the olive press; his Bible ran to about 180 copies in three years, and printed books at first imitated manuscripts with hand-painted decoration. (b) Erasmus welcomed print but feared that “a world of books” would let the bad drive out the good, and doubted that print would make people wiser. (c) The Act of 1878 allowed the government to censor Indian-language newspapers and to seize presses and property for “seditious” writing, while leaving English papers comparatively free.

3.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Write about the ways in which the print culture assisted the growth of nationalism in India.

Model answer

By creating a national public across languages and provinces; by carrying nationalist argument and news of movements in papers such as Kesari and Amrita Bazar Patrika; by spreading social reform and so creating a modern, self-critical public; by giving women, dalits and the poor a voice; and by making organisation possible through pamphlets, notices and petitions.

4.
NCERT exercise3 marks

How did print culture help in bringing about the Reformation in Europe?

Model answer

By circulating Luther’s Ninety Five Theses across Europe within weeks, by putting a German Bible in ordinary readers’ hands, and by creating a public of pamphlets and tracts in which reformers and the Church argued openly — which is why the Church replied with the Index of Prohibited Books in 1558.

5.
NCERT exercise5 marks

How did the printing press become a tool of social change in nineteenth-century India?

Model answer

It gave reformers — Ram Mohan Roy, Dayanand Saraswati, Vivekananda, Sir Syed Ahmed Khan — a means of public argument; it gave the excluded a platform, as in Phule’s Gulamgiri (1871), Ambedkar’s writings, Periyar’s Kudi Arasu and women’s autobiographies such as Amar Jiban (1876) and Stripurushtulna (1882); and it made reform arguments national, since a pamphlet printed in one province could be read in another.

6.
NCERT exercise3 marks

What did the spread of print in the nineteenth century mean to women, children and workers?

Model answer

Children gained a literature of their own, including the Grimm brothers’ fairy tales; women became readers and writers, with novels, magazines and, in India, autobiographies and polemics; workers gained cheap books, penny magazines, serialised novels, lending libraries and workers’ libraries. Print made reading a mass activity rather than an elite one.

7.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Describe the beginnings of print in China and Japan.

Model answer

In China, hand printing from woodblocks was known from about AD 594, and the imperial state printed examination textbooks in vast numbers; by the seventeenth century merchants, scholars and even courtesans used print. Buddhist missionaries took hand printing to Japan around AD 768–770 to print scriptures, and the oldest printed book there is the Diamond Sutra of AD 868; the Japanese used movable type in the late sixteenth century but woodblock printing remained common, producing the ukiyo prints of Utamaro and Hokusai.

8.
NCERT exercise3 marks

How did print reach Europe and what did Gutenberg contribute?

Model answer

Marco Polo brought knowledge of woodblock printing to Italy in 1295, and by the fifteenth century woodblock printing had spread. Gutenberg developed the printing press in the 1430s, using metal movable type, an oil-based ink and the mechanism of the olive press, and printed about 180 copies of the Bible in three years — making books cheap and abundant, and setting off the print revolution.

09

Important Questions and Answers

Board-style practice

Practice questions

Written in the style of CBSE board papers. They are additional practice, not NCERT originals.

1.

Describe the print revolution and its effects on European society. (5 marks)

Model answer

The print revolution was the shift from hand copying and woodblock printing to mechanical printing with movable type. Its effects were far-reaching. It created a new reading public: books became cheap, so readers multiplied beyond the elite, and between the literate and the illiterate grew an intermediate oral culture of printed ballads and tales read aloud. It produced cheap popular literature — chapbooks and the Bibliothèque Bleue — sold by pedlars. It transformed religion: Luther’s Ninety Five Theses of 1517 were printed and spread across Europe, his German Bible let ordinary people read the scriptures, and the Church replied with the Index of Prohibited Books in 1558. It created a public sphere of newspapers, journals and coffee-house debate, in which the ideas of the Enlightenment — and criticism of monarchy and Church — circulated; Diderot’s Encyclopaedia (from 1751) ran to 28 volumes. And it made possible new kinds of readers and reading: the Italian miller Menocchio read printed books and formed his own ideas, which brought him before the Inquisition. Print thus changed the relationship of readers to authority.

2.

Explain the “reading mania” of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. (5 marks)

Model answer

Print made reading a mass activity. Churches of different denominations set up village schools, so that by the mid-eighteenth century literacy rates in many parts of Europe reached 60 to 80 per cent. New forms of popular literature appeared for these new readers: almanacs and calendars carrying information about seasons, stars and weather together with entertainment; ballads and folk tales in cheap chapbooks sold by pedlars; the Bibliothèque Bleue in France; and newspapers and journals, read in coffee houses and aloud to the illiterate. Scholarly and scientific works were printed too — Newton’s work, and from 1751 Diderot’s Encyclopaedia in 28 volumes. The result was a public sphere in which ideas of reason, liberty and equality circulated widely, and historians link this reading mania to the Enlightenment and to the coming of the French Revolution.

3.

How did print change the lives of women, children and workers in the nineteenth century? (5 marks)

Model answer

Children gained a literature of their own: the Grimm brothers collected and published folk tales, and books were written specially for the young. Women became both readers and writers — Jane Austen, the Brontë sisters and George Eliot wrote novels read across Europe, and women contributed to magazines and journals; in India, Rashsundari Debi’s Amar Jiban (1876) and Tarabai Shinde’s Stripurushtulna (1882) opened a space in which women described their own lives. Workers gained access through cheap books, penny magazines, serialised novels, lending libraries and workers’ libraries, and print carried the arguments of the reform movements — anti-slavery, factory legislation, the vote and temperance. Reading ceased to be an elite privilege and became a mass activity, which is what made the great public campaigns of the century possible.

4.

Describe the growth of print in India from 1780 to 1878. (5 marks)

Model answer

India had a rich manuscript culture — hand-written on palm leaf and handmade paper in Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic and regional languages — but manuscripts were expensive, fragile and slow to copy. The Portuguese brought a press to Goa in the mid-sixteenth century, but the growth of the Indian press began with the British. James Augustus Hickey started the Bengal Gazette in 1780, the first newspaper in India. The decisive development was the vernacular press: Ram Mohan Roy’s Sambad Kaumudi (1821) and Mirat-ul-Akhbar (1822) were followed by papers in Bengali, Hindi, Marathi, Tamil and other languages. By the second half of the century the vernacular press carried news to readers who did not know English, created a public sphere for political and social debate, and gave voice to Indian opinion — through papers such as Kesari (Tilak), Amrita Bazar Patrika, The Hindu and The Tribune. The government’s response was the Vernacular Press Act of 1878.

5.

How did print help the reform movements and give voice to women and lower castes in India? (5 marks)

Model answer

Print made reform arguments public and repeatable. Ram Mohan Roy used his newspapers to campaign against sati; Dayanand Saraswati and Vivekananda published their views and reached wide audiences; the Deoband seminary (1867) printed fatwas for distribution, and Sir Syed Ahmed Khan published Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq to promote modern education. For the excluded, print was a platform: Jyotiba Phule’s Gulamgiri (1871) attacked caste and was dedicated to freed American slaves; Ambedkar wrote extensively against caste; Periyar published Kudi Arasu. For women, print created a space of their own — Rashsundari Debi’s Amar Jiban (1876), the first full-length autobiography in Bengali, Tarabai Shinde’s Stripurushtulna (1882), Pandita Ramabai’s writings on upper-caste Hindu women, and Kailashbashini Debi’s account of women imprisoned at home and kept in ignorance.

6.

Why did the colonial government pass the Vernacular Press Act? What does it tell us about print and nationalism? (5 marks)

Model answer

Because the vernacular press had become a powerful critic of British rule. Papers in Indian languages carried reports of grievances, campaigns and nationalist argument to a public that the English-language press did not reach, and the government saw this as sedition. The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 allowed it to censor reports and editorials, and to warn, seize the press and machinery, and confiscate the property of a paper judged “seditious”, while English-language papers were left comparatively free — a discrimination nationalists criticised bitterly. It shows that print and nationalism were bound together: the press created a national public and made organisation possible, and the state’s attempt to control it was an attempt to control the nation’s political life. Gandhiji made the connection explicit — the fight for Swaraj is a fight for liberty of speech, liberty of the press and freedom of association.

7.

What were the technical innovations that made print cheap and abundant? (3 marks)

Model answer

Richard Hoe’s power-driven printing press in the 1840s, the offset press, the linotype machine of the 1880s, photo-electric control and colour printing in the 1920s, and cheap paperbacks in the 1930s — together with cheaper paper and faster transport, which made mass circulation of newspapers and books possible.

8.

What was the Index of Prohibited Books and why was it issued? (3 marks)

Model answer

It was a list of books banned by the Catholic Church, first issued in 1558, after print allowed criticism of the Church to spread rapidly. It was an instrument of censorship — an attempt to control what people read and to suppress writings the Church considered heretical — and it shows that print had become a threat to established authority.

9.

How did print create a new reading public, and what was the role of oral culture? (5 marks)

Model answer

Before print, reading was confined to the elite and books were expensive; print made books cheap and multiplied readers. But the transition was gradual: in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries literacy was still limited, and between the literate and the illiterate grew an intermediate world of oral culture. Printed ballads, folk tales and chapbooks were sold by pedlars and read aloud in homes, markets and coffee houses, so that even those who could not read could participate in the new print culture. The oral and the printed fed on each other — printers collected folk tales and printed them, and the printed tales re-entered oral circulation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Quick clarifications

1.

Where was printing invented?

Model answer

In China — hand printing from woodblocks is known from about AD 594; Korea and Japan developed it further, and the oldest printed book, the Diamond Sutra, is Japanese, dated AD 868.

2.

What was Marco Polo’s contribution?

Model answer

He returned to Italy in 1295 after years in China and brought back knowledge of woodblock printing, which then spread in Europe.

3.

What did Gutenberg add to existing technology?

Model answer

Metal movable type, an oil-based ink, and the adaptation of the olive press into a printing press — making books cheap and fast to produce.

4.

What is a chapbook?

Model answer

A cheap small booklet of ballads, folk tales and popular stories, sold by pedlars.

5.

What is ukiyo?

Model answer

Japanese woodblock prints of urban life and the “floating world”, produced by artists such as Utamaro and Hokusai.

6.

Why was print feared?

Model answer

Because it could spread sedition, irreligion and rebellion; Erasmus feared “a world of books” in which the bad would drive out the good, and the Church banned books through the Index.

7.

What was a fatwa and how was print used?

Model answer

A legal opinion by an Islamic scholar; the Deoband seminary (1867) printed fatwas and distributed them to guide Muslims.

8.

What did Gandhiji say about the press?

Model answer

That the fight for Swaraj is a fight for liberty of speech, liberty of the press and freedom of association — political freedom and a free press cannot be separated.

Assertion-Reason Questions

Choose the correct option

How to answer

(a) Both A and R are true and R explains A. (b) Both are true but R does not explain A. (c) A is true, R is false. (d) A is false, R is true.

1.

Assertion (A): Woodblock printing was known in China from about AD 594.
Reason (R): Books were printed by rubbing paper against inked woodblocks.

2.

Assertion (A): Marco Polo brought the printing press to Europe.
Reason (R): He brought back knowledge of woodblock printing in 1295.

3.

Assertion (A): Gutenberg’s press made books cheap and abundant.
Reason (R): It used metal movable type and an oil-based ink.

4.

Assertion (A): Print helped the Reformation.
Reason (R): Luther’s Ninety Five Theses were printed and circulated widely.

5.

Assertion (A): The Catholic Church welcomed the spread of printed criticism.
Reason (R): It maintained an Index of Prohibited Books from 1558.

6.

Assertion (A): The vernacular press helped the growth of nationalism in India.
Reason (R): It carried nationalist argument to readers who did not know English.

7.

Assertion (A): The Vernacular Press Act treated English and Indian-language papers equally.
Reason (R): English-language papers were left comparatively free.

8.

Assertion (A): Print gave women in India a space to describe their own lives.
Reason (R): Amar Jiban and Stripurushtulna were published in the 1870s and 1880s.

9.

Assertion (A): Print reduced the importance of oral culture.
Reason (R): Printed ballads and tales were read aloud to the illiterate.

10.

Assertion (A): Print made censorship unnecessary.
Reason (R): The colonial state passed the Vernacular Press Act in 1878.

Source-Based and Case-Based Questions

Read the passage or table, then answer

Source 1 — Gutenberg and the printed Bible

Source extract

Johannes Gutenberg grew up in a large agricultural estate and learnt the art of polishing stones, became a master goldsmith, and acquired expertise in creating lead moulds. By 1448 he had perfected his system. He used his knowledge to design movable type, and adapted the existing technology of the olive press to make a printing press. He used an oil-based ink and a metal mould to cast type. His first printed book was the Bible: about 180 copies in three years.

1.

What existing skills and technologies did Gutenberg combine?

Model answer

Stone polishing, goldsmithing and the casting of lead moulds; and he adapted the olive press. With an oil-based ink and metal movable type he turned these into a printing press.

2.

Why was 180 copies in three years remarkable?

Model answer

Because a single handwritten copy of a Bible could take years to produce; the press multiplied output enormously and lowered the cost per copy.

3.

Why did printed books at first imitate manuscripts?

Model answer

Because the new technology had to win acceptance in a market used to manuscripts: metal letters imitated ornamental handwriting, borders were illuminated by hand, and space was left for buyers to choose decoration. The form of the book changed more slowly than its method of production.

Source 2 — Luther and print

Source extract

Martin Luther was in favour of print and spoke out in praise of it. In 1517 he wrote Ninety Five Theses criticising many of the practices and rituals of the Roman Catholic Church. A printed copy of this was posted on a church door in Wittenberg. It challenged the Church to debate his ideas. Luther’s writings were immediately reproduced in vast numbers and read widely. This led to a division within the Church and to the beginning of the Protestant Reformation. Luther said, “Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one.”

1.

How did the Theses become a public challenge?

Model answer

By being printed and posted on a church door in Wittenberg, and then reproduced in vast numbers and read widely — print turned a scholarly objection into a public call for debate.

2.

Why did Luther call printing the greatest gift of God?

Model answer

Because it let his criticism of the Church and his German translation of the Bible reach ordinary people directly, without the mediation of priests — the instrument of the Reformation.

3.

What did the Church do in response?

Model answer

It tried to control what was printed: from 1558 it maintained an Index of Prohibited Books and suppressed writings it considered heretical.

Source 3 — Print and Indian nationalism

Source extract

Gandhiji said that the fight for Swaraj is a fight for liberty of speech, liberty of the press, and freedom of association. The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 had allowed the government to censor reports and editorials in the vernacular press. If a vernacular newspaper published anything that was considered seditious, the government could warn the editor, seize the press and machinery, and confiscate the property. English-language newspapers were left comparatively free.

1.

Why did Gandhiji link the freedom of the press to Swaraj?

Model answer

Because political freedom depends on the ability to speak, publish and organise. Without a free press Indians could not criticise the government, spread arguments or build a movement — so the fight for self-rule was necessarily a fight for these freedoms.

2.

What did the Vernacular Press Act reveal about colonial policy?

Model answer

That the government feared Indian-language opinion far more than English-language opinion: it censored the vernacular press while leaving English papers comparatively free, which nationalists saw as a discrimination against Indian political life.

3.

How does censorship relate to the chapter’s larger argument?

Model answer

Print created a public sphere; censorship is the attempt to close it. The history of print is therefore also the history of the struggle for freedom of expression — from the Index of Prohibited Books to the Vernacular Press Act.

Make a table of five newspapers of nineteenth-century India with their language and founder.

3.

Prepare a chart of the print technology innovations from 1430 to 1930.

Model answer

Gutenberg’s press (1430s) → wooden hand press → iron press → Richard Hoe’s power-driven press (1840s) → offset press → linotype (1880s) → photo-electric control and colour printing (1920s) → cheap paperback (1930s).

HOTS and Competency-Based Questions

Think beyond the text

Higher order thinking

These ask you to apply, compare or evaluate. Model answers are indicative — your own well-reasoned answer can differ.

1.

“Print did not merely spread ideas; it changed the kind of ideas that could exist.” Discuss.

Model answer

Yes. Print made ideas repeatable and comparable: an argument once printed could be read by strangers in other towns, checked, quoted and answered, which produced a public sphere of debate rather than isolated opinion. It made ideas cheap, so they reached readers beyond the elite, and it made them fast, so that Luther’s Theses could travel across Europe in weeks. It also created new genres — the newspaper, the journal, the encyclopaedia, the novel — each of which shapes what can be said. And it made possible the modern idea of a public that holds power to account. (Model answer.)

2.

Why did the same technology produce the Reformation in Europe and anti-colonial nationalism in India?

Model answer

Because print is a technology of circulation, and what it circulates depends on the questions of the society it enters. In sixteenth-century Europe the central question was religious authority, and print carried Luther’s challenge to the Church. In nineteenth-century India the central question was colonial rule and social reform, and print carried the arguments of reformers, of women, of dalits and of nationalists. The technology was the same; the public and its grievances were different — which is why the same press produced the Index of Prohibited Books in one place and the Vernacular Press Act in another. (Model answer.)

3.

Was the colonial government right to fear the vernacular press?

Model answer

From its own point of view, yes: the vernacular press reached a far larger public than English papers, carried criticism of colonial policy into the interior, and helped organise movements. But the fear reveals the political importance of print rather than any wrongdoing by editors: the Vernacular Press Act censored Indian-language papers while leaving English papers comparatively free, which was discrimination, not security. Gandhiji’s formulation — that Swaraj is a fight for liberty of speech, of the press and of association — states the principle the Act violated. (Model answer.)

4.

How did print change the position of women in nineteenth-century India?

Model answer

It gave some women the chance to write and be read, and others the chance to read about lives like their own. Rashsundari Debi learnt to read in secret and published Amar Jiban (1876); Tarabai Shinde compared the condition of women and men in Stripurushtulna (1882); Pandita Ramabai wrote about upper-caste Hindu women and founded a widow’s home; Kailashbashini Debi described women imprisoned at home and kept in ignorance. Print created a space for women’s testimony, and it also created a readership for arguments about reform — though it did not by itself change the conditions it described. (Model answer.)

5.

Is the printed book still the most important medium? What has changed since 1930?

Model answer

The printed book remains important but is no longer the only or even the dominant medium. Radio, cinema, television and now the internet have taken over much of the work print once did — news, entertainment, debate — and digital media have changed the economics of publishing: anyone can circulate text at almost no cost, and circulation is instantaneous and global. But the underlying questions the chapter raises remain: who can publish, who can read, and who tries to control what circulates. Those questions have simply moved to new platforms. (Model answer.)

6.

Why does the chapter end with censorship rather than with technology?

Model answer

Because the point of the chapter is not machines but publics. Print matters because it created readers who could judge, argue and organise — and the test of that public is whether it is free. The Index of Prohibited Books and the Vernacular Press Act show that authority recognised this: censorship is the compliment power pays to the printed word. Ending with censorship, and with Gandhiji’s linking of the press to Swaraj, makes the argument that print culture and political freedom are one history. (Model answer.)

Reading mania

  • Literacy 60–80% in parts of Europe by mid-18th century.
  • Almanacs, ballads, newspapers, coffee houses; Diderot’s Encyclopaedia from 1751 (28 vols).

19th century

  • Children: Grimm’s tales. Women: Austen, Brontës, Eliot. Workers: penny magazines, serialised novels, libraries.
  • Innovations: Hoe’s press (1840s), offset, linotype (1880s), colour (1920s), paperbacks (1930s).

India

  • Manuscript culture: palm leaf, Sanskrit/Persian/Arabic; Portuguese press in Goa.
  • 1780 Bengal Gazette (Hickey); 1821 Sambad Kaumudi; 1822 Mirat-ul-Akhbar.
  • Kesari (Tilak), Amrita Bazar Patrika, The Hindu, The Tribune.

Reform and voices

  • Ram Mohan Roy, Dayanand, Vivekananda; Deoband 1867 fatwas; Sir Syed’s Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq.
  • Phule’s Gulamgiri 1871; Ambedkar; Periyar’s Kudi Arasu.
  • Rashsundari Debi’s Amar Jiban 1876; Tarabai Shinde’s Stripurushtulna 1882; Pandita Ramabai.

Censorship

  • Vernacular Press Act 1878 — censor, seize, confiscate; English papers freer.
  • Gandhiji: Swaraj is a fight for liberty of speech, of the press and of association.
19

Chapter Summary

The whole chapter in a few paragraphs

Print began in China, where hand printing from woodblocks was known from about AD 594 and the imperial state printed examination textbooks in vast numbers. Buddhist missionaries carried the technique to Japan around AD 768–770; the oldest printed book there is the Diamond Sutra of AD 868, and by the eighteenth century a lively urban culture produced the ukiyo prints of Utamaro and Hokusai. Marco Polo brought knowledge of woodblock printing to Italy in 1295, and by the fifteenth century it had spread through Europe — though luxury books were still handwritten on expensive vellum.

Gutenberg’s printing press of the 1430s — metal movable type, oil-based ink and the mechanism of the olive press — made books cheap and abundant: his Bible ran to about 180 copies in three years, and between 1450 and 1550 presses were set up across Europe, with 20 million books in the second half of the fifteenth century and about 200 million in the sixteenth. The print revolution created a new reading public and an intermediate oral culture of ballads and chapbooks; it carried Luther’s Ninety Five Theses of 1517 across Europe and helped produce the Reformation, to which the Church replied with the Index of Prohibited Books in 1558. The seventeenth and eighteenth centuries saw a “reading mania” — almanacs, ballads, newspapers and journals, with literacy reaching 60 to 80 per cent in places and Diderot’s Encyclopaedia appearing from 1751. In the nineteenth century print reached children, women and workers, and technical innovations made it ever cheaper.

In India, a rich manuscript culture preceded print. The Portuguese brought a press to Goa in the sixteenth century, but the growth of the Indian press began with Hickey’s Bengal Gazette in 1780 and, decisively, with the vernacular press — Ram Mohan Roy’s Sambad Kaumudi (1821) and Mirat-ul-Akhbar (1822), followed by Kesari, Amrita Bazar Patrika, The Hindu and The Tribune. Print carried religious and social reform, gave women and lower castes a voice — Phule’s Gulamgiri (1871), Rashsundari Debi’s Amar Jiban (1876), Tarabai Shinde’s Stripurushtulna (1882) — and became a weapon of nationalism.

The colonial state replied with the Vernacular Press Act of 1878, censoring Indian-language papers while leaving English ones comparatively free. Gandhiji’s statement that the fight for Swaraj is a fight for liberty of speech, liberty of the press and freedom of association states the chapter’s conclusion: print created a public, and freedom is the condition of that public’s existence.
